extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning elementary set theory, quantificational logic, and proof writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for translating set-theoretic notation into quantified logical formulas and for composing correct, well-justified mathematical proofs (strategies, style, and common transformations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set elementhood (P(X) definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The elements of P(A) are precisely the subsets of A; to say x ∈ P(A) means x ⊆ A, which can be written as ∀y (y ∈ x → y ∈ A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this translation when expanding occurrences of power-set notation. Example translations in the text: x ∈ P(A) ↔ x ⊆ A ↔ ∀y(y ∈ x → y ∈ A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subset relation translation
rubrics_metrics.description: A ⊆ B (or x ⊆ A) is to be written out as a universal quantification: ∀y (y ∈ A → y ∈ B) (or ∀y (y ∈ x → y ∈ A)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a statement involves a subset relation, expand with the definition of subset before or after other definitions as appropriate; the text shows using this in multi-step translations (e.g., expressing P(A) containment relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection and union of a family (NF and UF definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is a family of sets, NF = {x | ∀A ∈ F (x ∈ A)} and UF = {x | ∃A ∈ F (x ∈ A)}. These are the generalizations of pairwise intersection and union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating membership statements involving NF or UF, replace 'x ∈ NF' by '∀A ∈ F (x ∈ A)' and 'x ∈ UF' by '∃A ∈ F (x ∈ A)'. Note: some mathematicians consider NF undefined when F = ∅; the text avoids NF unless F ≠ ∅. Also, if F = ∅ then x ∈ UF is always false, so UF = ∅.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed-family notation translation
rubrics_metrics.description: For indexed families {A_i | i ∈ I}, use notation: ⋂_{i∈I} A_i = {x | ∀i ∈ I (x ∈ A_i)} and ⋃_{i∈I} A_i = {x | ∃i ∈ I (x ∈ A_i)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may rewrite indexed unions/intersections into the family-quantifier form when translating to logical symbols; examples include translating N_{i∈J} A_i and U_{i∈J} A_i into explicit quantifiers over the index set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with the outermost symbol when expanding definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating a complex mathematical statement into logical symbols, begin by expanding the definition of the outermost symbol (the 'rule of thumb' given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: For x ∈ P(A ∩ B) expand P(...) first (so you get x ⊆ A ∩ B), while for (x ∈ P(A)) ∩ (x ∈ P(B)) you might expand intersection first. Choosing the appropriate order simplifies the translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use logical equivalences and quantifier-negation laws when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing out definitions you may need to apply logical equivalences and quantifier negation (e.g., ¬∃ ↔ ∀¬) to get statements into the required form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text demonstrates rewriting 'x ∉ U_G' into ∀A ∈ G (x ∉ A) via quantifier negation and using equivalences to remove set-theory shorthand when restricted symbol sets are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate compound set expressions stepwise and flexibly
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single required order for expanding nested set-theoretic constructs; choose an order (outermost-first is a good rule) that simplifies the work, and be prepared to expand subset, union, intersection, power set definitions as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examples show doing intersection-first in some cases and power-set-first in others; both can yield equivalent final logical formulas. Be mindful of equivalences and try to minimize complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing equality or set identities by elementhood tests
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove set equalities (or membership equivalences) translate 'x ∈ S' and 'x ∈ T' into logical formulas and show the two formulas are equivalent (i.e., show x ∈ S ↔ x ∈ T for arbitrary x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book suggests proving P(A ∩ B) = P(A) ∩ P(B) by comparing the translations for an arbitrary x; use this elementwise method to prove many set identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs must cover all instances; use counterexamples to disprove
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorem with free variables is only correct if for every instance where the hypotheses hold the conclusion holds. A single instance where the hypotheses hold and the conclusion fails is a counterexample and disproves the theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When checking a purported theorem, either produce a proof valid for arbitrary instances or exhibit a counterexample; the text gives a numeric counterexample to show an incorrect theorem fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never assert anything before it is fully justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not claim a statement as true in a proof until it has been completely justified using the hypotheses or previously proven conclusions. 'I shall make no assertion before its time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents circular reasoning and unwarranted leaps. Be skeptical of every inference and ensure each step follows from givens or earlier steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish assumptions from assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming a statement temporarily (for the sake of argument) is different from asserting it as true; assumptions allow you to derive conditionals (e.g., to prove P → Q assume P and derive Q), but you must not present assumptions as established facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep clear when a line is an assumption used to derive a conditional goal versus when a line is a justified assertion to be used later without caveat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bookkeeping: track givens and the current goal
rubrics_metrics.description: While devising a proof, keep a list of the statements known or assumed at that point (givens) and the statement currently to be proven (goal); transformations change givens and goal in controlled ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses 'givens' and 'goal' to describe intermediate transformed problems and shows how strategies modify them; record these changes to guide the construction of the rest of the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy for proving a conditional (P → Q): assume P and prove Q
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal of the form P → Q, temporarily assume P, add it to the givens, and then prove Q. Final form: 'Suppose P. [Proof of Q.] Therefore P → Q.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book gives both 'scratch work' bookkeeping and the recommended final proof template. Use this when the direct conditional approach is natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative strategy: prove a conditional via its contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Since P → Q is equivalent to ¬Q → ¬P, you may prove P → Q by assuming ¬Q and proving ¬P. Final form: 'Suppose ¬Q. [Proof of ¬P.] Therefore P → Q.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try the contrapositive when assuming P directly is hard; the text illustrates choosing between the direct conditional strategy and the contrapositive by trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose proof strategies guided by the logical forms of hypotheses and conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The logical form of the goal and of the hypotheses suggests appropriate proof techniques (e.g., conditional goals suggest assuming antecedents; universal goals suggest arbitrary-instance proofs; existentials suggest constructing a witness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no single recipe; often try several strategies. With practice you will better guess which strategy is likely to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final write-up conventions: concise, minimal thought-process, natural language
rubrics_metrics.description: The final written proof should usually omit scratch-work and excessive commentary about how you found the proof; state the key assumptions and deductions succinctly in ordinary English rather than heavy logical symbolism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include brief sentences to indicate transformations (e.g., 'Suppose P') but do not present the entire exploratory process. In complicated proofs you may include a short explanation of strategy for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: When manipulating inequalities, attend to signs when multiplying/dividing
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic steps in proofs (e.g., multiplying both sides of an inequality) require checking conditions (such as positivity of multipliers) to ensure direction of inequality is preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examples show multiplying by positive numbers to preserve order; always state relevant hypotheses (e.g., 0 < a < b) that permit such operations safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and experimentation to find conjectures, but proofs are required for certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimentation, trial and error, and examples can guide conjecture formation or help find a proof path, but a deductive proof is required to be convinced of a theorem's correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat a checked instance as a proof; instead use experimentation as scratch work and then supply a full proof that covers all instances.
